title: EASA and EUROCONTROL publish joint Action Plan to ensure safe operations during GNSS interference events
date_evidence: COLOGNE/BRUSSELS, March 26, 2026 - EASA and EUROCONTROL published a joint Action Plan to strengthen the safety and resilience of European aviation operations amid the growing challenge of GNSS interference.
key_claim: EASA and EUROCONTROL published a joint Action Plan setting out short, mid and longer-term measures to mitigate GNSS interference with harmonised operational procedures, including minimum requirements for GNSS interference monitoring tools (a 2026 deliverable) and harmonised criteria defining who needs to act and by when.
frame_summary: This source argues that GNSS interference has become a persistent aviation-safety threat requiring a coordinated European regulatory response with defined actors and deadlines.
notes: Tier 1 regulator / multilateral. Structural anchor for the regulator-response framing (26 March 2026, just outside the 3-month window).

publisher: U.S. House Committee on Energy and Commerce
title: Chairman Hudson opening statement, Communications and Technology Subcommittee hearing on Positioning, Navigation, and Timing Capabilities
date_evidence: Jun 04, 2026 [Communications & Technology][Press Release] - Chairman Hudson delivers opening statement at the PNT capabilities hearing.
key_claim: At a June 2026 Congressional hearing on positioning, navigation and timing, the chairman noted that just two weeks earlier a Royal Air Force jet carrying the United Kingdom's Defence Minister lost its GPS signal to suspected Russian jamming, and that the United States still has no congressionally mandated backup to GPS despite FCC steps such as a Notice of Inquiry into complementary systems.
frame_summary: This source argues the United States lacks a mandated GPS backup and that positioning, navigation and timing resilience is now an urgent Congressional and regulatory priority.
notes: Tier 1 US government primary statement. Anchors the policy-inflection and no-mandated-backup point.

title: Global Counterspace Capabilities: An Open Source Assessment (2026)
date_evidence: Secure World Foundation, Global Counterspace Capabilities 2026, published April 8, 2026, with an information cut-off of 28 February 2026; assesses electronic-warfare and other counterspace capabilities across 13 countries.
key_claim: The Secure World Foundation's 2026 Global Counterspace Capabilities assessment finds that GNSS jamming and spoofing have become a constant of modern conflict, documenting electronic-warfare capabilities across 13 countries and a spread of interference from northern Europe to the eastern Mediterranean.
frame_summary: This source argues that space and navigation electronic warfare, including GNSS jamming and spoofing, has normalised as a routine feature of contemporary conflict rather than an exceptional event.
notes: Tier 2 think-tank open-source assessment. Anchors the normalisation-of-interference framing. Exact publication day from web search.

title: How electronic warfare is sowing confusion in cockpits
date_evidence: Published Apr 28, 2026, 7:30 AM ET - report on GPS jamming and aircraft navigation problems.
key_claim: Around 900 flights each day are affected by GPS interference, according to SkAI Data Services; IFALPA represents over 160,000 pilots in more than 70 countries; Finland's Traficom received 421 reports of GPS reception interference in January and February 2026 after 1,704 in the whole of the previous year; and interference is implicated in an Azerbaijan Airlines crash that killed at least 38 of the 67 people on board.
frame_summary: This source argues that GPS jamming and spoofing have moved from a rare edge-of-conflict nuisance to a routine and safety-critical hazard for commercial aviation.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism. Primary source for the aviation scale figures (900 flights/day; Finland 421 vs 1,704; 160,000 pilots; 38 of 67).

title: GPS jamming attacks threaten critical sectors
key_claim: Maritime analytics firm Windward recorded over 1,100 vessels experiencing GPS interference in a single day in March 2026 and spotted 21 new AIS jamming clusters across the waters of the UAE, Qatar, Oman and Iran; spoofing reports more than doubled between January and June 2025; and approximately 700 jamming or spoofing events occurred every day in 2024, with critical sectors including telecoms, power and finance dependent on GNSS timing.
frame_summary: This source argues that GNSS jamming has escalated into a threat to critical civil sectors well beyond aviation, including maritime, telecoms, power and finance that rely on GNSS timing.
notes: Tier 3 trade press. Primary source for maritime and critical-sector scale (1,100 vessels; 700 events/day 2024).

title: The Epidemic of GPS Jamming
date_evidence: Foreign Policy, 'The Epidemic of GPS Jamming', published 1 June 2026 (URL path /2026/06/01/), on jamming across the Baltic, Black Sea, Red Sea and Persian Gulf.
key_claim: GPS jamming and spoofing have spread from the Baltic to the Black Sea, Red Sea, Gulf of Oman, Eastern Mediterranean and Persian Gulf; on 21 May 2026 the aircraft carrying the UK Defence Secretary was jammed for the duration of a flight from Estonia, and one aviation-security specialist described navigational interference as having gone from occasional to basically constant.
frame_summary: This source argues GPS jamming has become a widespread, cross-theatre condition affecting aviation and shipping across multiple regions rather than an isolated Baltic problem.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism, paywalled; used directionally for the geographic-spread framing, not for numeric anchors.

title: GPS Jamming is a Wake-Up Call for America
key_claim: The National Association of Broadcasters argues a significant GPS disruption could cost hundreds of billions of dollars in economic damage, and reports that it secured a Department of Transportation contract to test the Broadcast Positioning System for critical-infrastructure resilience and spun off a new company, Merkhet Solutions, to provide a broadcast-based backup to GPS.
frame_summary: This source argues that terrestrial broadcast-based positioning and timing is a viable, deployable backup to GPS that the United States should adopt for critical-infrastructure resilience.
notes: Tier 4 advocacy / practitioner (broadcast industry body). Used only as directional corroboration for the terrestrial-backup adaptation.
